title: Watched an AI agent go from +118% to +6% in three sessions on a public paper-trading leaderboard. It's still all-in on the call that did it.
author: Accomplished_Fun_408
selftext:
Disclosure: I work at RockFlow. We run a public arena where AI agents trade $1M of paper money each through our MCP, 10 agents on the board right now. This is not my agent. I can see every fill and the equity curve because the leaderboard is public; I can't see its prompt or its reasoning. All numbers below are paper.

The agent shows up as "Jeff BeZos". It joined on day one, July 21.

Act 1, July 21 to Aug 18: stocks only. NVDA, SMCI, COIN, MSTR, PLTR, a lot of churn. Down 11.5% at the low on July 31, hovering around −7% for three weeks.

Act 2, Aug 31: it buys $1.03M of TSLA Sept-18 $365 calls. That was 97% of the account. Next day the account closes at $618K, down 42% in one session. It holds. Sept 3 it sells for $1.17M, +$141K. It got paid for not flinching, and I think that's where the story turns.

Act 3, Sept 10 to 18: short-dated single-name options, both sides. Sept 10 it puts $794K into COIN puts and loses 58% of it. Same minute it dumps those on Sept 14, it sells BE puts it bought three days earlier for +$647K. Sept 16 to 17, BE calls +$455K. Sept 18 to 21, COIN calls +$151K. Peak on Sept 18 at 11:10 ET: $2.18M, +118%. Over the whole run: 26 closed option trades, 18 winners, 6 losers, realized +$1.25M on options and +$103K on stocks.

Act 4, Sept 21, 9:32 ET, two minutes after taking the COIN profit: one fill, $2,316,000 of CRCL Oct-16 $105 calls at $6.00. That's 100% of the account, $156 of cash left. CRCL closed that day at $94.49, then $94.59, then $91.72. By Wednesday's close the calls were at $2.74, unrealized −$1.26M, −54%, and the account was back to $1.06M, +5.8%. Thursday CRCL bounced to $93 and the calls to $3.04, so the board shows +17% right now. Same single position, still −49%, still 100% of the account, not one order placed since. For the calls to break even at expiry CRCL needs to be above about $111, +19% from here, with 16 sessions left including today.

Three things I take from the log:

1. Win rate was never the problem. 18 of 26. Position size was. The three biggest positions were 97%, 58% and 100% of the account, and they were also the only three that could end the run.

2. Getting paid for holding a 42% drawdown taught it the wrong lesson. Every all-in after that was bigger than the last: $1.03M, then $2.32M.

3. None of this exists in the real market. The CRCL position is 3,860 contracts. Open interest on that strike is 3,626 for the entire market. Paper fills at the screen price with no slippage make the whole curve, the rise and the fall, bigger than it could ever be with money.

We're adding hard caps at the account level for the next round. Genuine question for people running agents against a broker: do you enforce position limits in the prompt, in the tool schema, or in the account itself? The prompt clearly didn't hold here, if there was one.

comments.author: leroylabs
comments.body:
I'd enforce limits in a deterministic order gateway outside the agent's control, with broker/account restrictions where supported. The prompt can explain the policy; the gateway must reject violations. For that $2.316M CRCL call purchase, cap total option premium at risk relative to equity and reserve capacity for pending orders atomically, so simultaneous MCP calls can't each spend the same allowance.

The 3,860 contracts versus 3,626 open interest flags a fill-model question, but open interest isn't an executable-size ceiling. Available quotes, depth and price impact are what need checking. Also, without its prompt or reasoning, the TSLA recovery doesn't establish that it learned to hold through losses. Does every order path pass through the same limit check?

replies.author: Accomplished_Fun_408
replies.body:
Agreed on the gateway, and thanks for the premium-at-risk framing. Notional caps are the wrong unit for options; a cap on premium at risk as a share of equity is what I'll push for. The atomic reservation point I hadn't considered at all. An agent that fires parallel tool calls could pass the same stale check several times, and nothing in the log rules that out.

On your question: as far as I know, every order path, app or MCP, hits the same order service and the same check, and that check is buying power at the account level. No premium-at-risk cap, no per-underlying cap. That's exactly what let a 100% position through. Whether concurrent orders reserve against buying power atomically, I don't know, and I'd rather ask the trading team than guess here. Will report back.

Fair on both corrections. OI isn't a ceiling, it's just the number that made me stop and look; the real problem is that our paper engine fills any size at the quote with no depth model. And "it learned to hold" is my reading of two data points, not evidence. Without the prompt, everything I wrote is a story told about a trade log.

replies.author: Shoddy_Peanut7320
replies.body:
Re "Watched an AI agent go from +118% to +6% in three sessions on a public paper-trading leaderboard. It's still all-in on the call that did it.":

"Fully agree on the deterministic gateway point, and the atomic-reservation detail is the one people miss most, a naive 'check remaining allowance, then submit' pattern has an obvious race condition the moment an agent (or multiple agents) can issue concurrent calls, you need the reservation and the check to be a single atomic operation or you get exactly the kind of blown-through-the-cap scenario that no prompt-level policy would ever catch. Good catch separating open interest from executable size too, that's a common conflation, OI tells you how much exists, not how much you can actually fill without moving the price against yourself, real depth/impact modeling is the only honest ceiling, especially once paper fills stop reflecting what a real order book could absorb. On whether every order path hits the same limit check: that's really the core architectural question for any agent-broker system, if there's more than one entry point (direct tool call, scheduled job, manual override) and even one of them bypasses the gateway, the whole guarantee collapses, so the safest design treats the gateway as the only path to the broker, full stop, not just the default one.

This exact separation, deterministic risk/execution gateway with the AI kept out of the loop for sizing and limits, is the architecture EventTrader's agent hookup is built around too, this kind of failure case is a pretty clean illustration of why."
